chunks: And informed us Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Salama ibn al-Khattab, from Ali ibn Hassaan, from Abdurrahman ibn Kathir, who said:

I was with Abu Abdillah when Muhzim entered upon him, and he said to him: 'May I be your ransom, inform me about this matter which we are waiting for, when is it?' He said: 'O Muhzim, the diviners have lied, the hasteners have perished, and the Muslims were saved.'

key_terms.الْأَمْرُ: The Matter, referring to the reappearance of the Mahdi.
key_terms.الْمُسْتَعْجِلُونَ: The hasteners, those who rush or expect immediate fulfillment, who perish.
key_terms.الْمُسْلِمُونَ: The Muslims, those who patiently wait and are saved.
key_terms.الْوَقَّاتُونَ: The diviners/those who set specific times, who are described as liars.
key_terms.مُهْزَمٌ: Muhzim, a specific companion or figure known for asking about the timing of the event.

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the three groups mentioned by Imam al-Sadiq regarding the waiting for the Mahdi?
ai.summary: In this narration from Al-Nu'mani's *Kitab al-Ghayba*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses the common Shia anxiety regarding the precise timing of the Mahdi's reappearance by categorizing the community into three distinct spiritual states. He highlights that while 'diviners' (al-Waqqatun) who fixate on specific dates are ultimately false, and 'hasteners' (al-Mustajilun) who rush ahead of divine decree perish, true salvation belongs to the 'Muslims' (al-Muslimun) who maintain steadfast patience and readiness. This distinction underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on *al-intizar* (expectant patience) as an active state of spiritual preparedness rather than mere passive waiting or chronological speculation.
